messages.text: What are the main findings of this paper?

messages.short_answer: The paper finds that non-AI experts explored prompts opportunistically rather than systematically, and struggled in ways that echo end-user programming and interactive machine learning, largely because human-to-human instruction expectations and a tendency to overgeneralize from few observations hindered effective prompt design.

sections.title: Core findings from the abstract
sections.text: The authors report that probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and that expectations from human-to-human instruction and a tendency to overgeneralize were barriers to effective prompt design. They frame these findings as having implications for LLM-based tool design and for LLM-and-prompt literacy.

sections.title: Specific behaviours seen in the 10-participant study
sections.text: According to PaperLens's overview of the study pages, most participants declared success after a single instance, relied on local testing, and rarely used error labeling or systematic testing. Participants also struggled more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and often used 'do not' phrasing even though 'do' phrasing was more effective.

sections.title: Mismatch between expectations and LLM behaviour
sections.text: The authors report that participants expected semantically equivalent instructions to give equivalent results, while trivial prompt changes often produced large shifts in conversations. Users also frequently could not explain why the model behaved as it did, which the authors link to LLM black-box opacity.

sections.title: Relevance to your PhD study
sections.text: Your planned study of how non-experts write prompts overlaps closely with the paper's observed behaviours, so its findings could serve as hypotheses or a comparison baseline. A possible adaptation would be to define your own measures of systematic testing and robustness, since the paper's sample was small, academic, and early-adopter, and its tool used GPT-3 text-davinci-002. Whether this fits your design is your decision to make.

sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages describe a user study of non-expert participants writing prompts for an LLM-based chatbot playing the character Carla. They report participants' misconceptions, such as expecting the bot to remember past conversations or be unaffected by a hard reset, and their social, polite phrasing of instructions (e.g., starting with "please"). The pages also cover participants' bias toward direct instruction over examples, reluctance to copy transcript dialog despite observed gains, and difficulty finding and applying web help. Finally, they note that participants struggled much more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and collected data opportunistically rather than systematically.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

Why Johnny Can’t Prompt CHI ’23, April 23–28, 2023, Hamburg, Germany to P4’s surprise. After P4 tried a few variations over a few minutes— adding quotation marks, changing punctuation, etc.—the interviewer fnally suggested trying a do-focused form of the instruction, which P4 initially appended after the “Don’t [...]” instruction, again without success. Removing the “Don’t [...]” instruction fnally resolved this particular error. This example illustrates two of the mismatches between human expectations about instruction-giving and the realities of LLM prompting. First, our participants expected that plain descriptions of behavior should be “understood” and acted upon, and if they aren’t, it refects LLM capabilities. Second, our participants expected that semantically equivalent instructions would have semantically equivalent results, while in reality trivial modifcations to a prompt can lead to dramatic shifts in future unfolding of conversations.

sources.text: These pages discuss a study of how end-users prompt LLM-based chatbots (GPT-3), focusing on mismatches between users' expectations and LLM behavior. Participants were surprised that trivial prompt changes, such as rephrasing or adding a negated 'Don't' instruction, could produce dramatically different outputs, and that plain behavioral descriptions were not always followed. The authors note that participants could rarely explain why the model behaved as it did, given the black-box nature of LLMs. The discussion then offers implications for training and education, including encouraging users to collect more data and perform systematic testing, and suggests searchable example repositories and explanations of instruction time horizons. The pages end by raising design opportunities, such as heuristics for how much data or how many conversations are needed for robustness testing.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

sections.title: Where the method could help your study
sections.text: The paper's probe approach, in which non-experts iterate on prompts for a chatbot with think-aloud and interviewer observation, maps closely onto a study of how non-expert users write prompts. The paper's six-category framing (design, selection, coordination, use, understanding, information barriers) could also serve as a coding scheme for your observations.

sections.title: What the paper itself provides
sections.text: The authors report that ten non-expert participants explored prompts opportunistically and tended to overgeneralize from single observations, and that the study used think-aloud while participants improved a baseline chatbot. They also state that expectations from human-to-human instruction shaped how participants wrote prompts. One reported mismatch is that participants expected semantically equivalent instructions to yield equivalent results, while trivial edits often produced large shifts.

sections.title: Limitations for your study
sections.text: The authors themselves note that the participant pool skewed toward STEM professionals and graduate students and is not representative, and that interviewer advice varied across participants. The study used one task (a cooking chatbot), one model (GPT-3 text-davinci-002), and a limited prompt-design time. Findings may not transfer to other populations, non-chatbot domains, or newer models.

sections.title: What you would need before relying on it
sections.text: Before adopting the probe or its findings, you would likely need to justify your own population and task, decide how consistently to give interviewer hints, and consider whether a newer model changes the observed behaviours. Piloting the protocol with your target users would also help check that the think-aloud and task design work for your research questions.

sections.text: The authors used a design probe to observe 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience, and report that end-users explore prompts opportunistically but struggle to make systematic progress. They also justify building a dedicated prompt design tool because existing tools focus on experimentation rather than robust, generalizable prompts.

sources.text: Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. This paper makes three contributions.

sources.text: We chose to create a design probe because the robustness of prompt strategies is highly dependent on specifc conversational contexts, as is users’ ability to create prompts and debug. Enabling people to engage in designing LLM-and-prompt-based chatbots hands-on offers deeper insights than conducting interviews about hypothetical scenarios alone. We chose to purpose-build a prompt design tool because existing tools focus on enabling non-experts to experiment with various prompting strategies rather than crafting robust and generalizable prompts. 3.1 Designing a No-Code Prompt Design Tool as Probe Design Goals. We have two goals in designing BotDesigner: First, to enable end-users, without any prompt design experience or even programming or ML experience, to (i) create a chatbot using prompts, without code, and (ii) systematically evaluate their prompts. Second, to allow end-users to engage in this process in a fexible, open-ended way, allowing us to observe their intuitive behaviors and thought processes.

sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages describe a user study of non-expert participants writing prompts for an LLM-based chatbot playing the character Carla. They report participants' misconceptions, such as expecting the bot to remember past conversations or be unaffected by a hard reset, and their social, polite phrasing of instructions (e.g., starting with "please"). The pages also cover participants' bias toward direct instruction over examples, reluctance to copy transcript dialog despite observed gains, and difficulty finding and applying web help. Finally, they note that participants struggled much more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and collected data opportunistically rather than systematically.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. Why Johnny Can’t Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts J.D. Zamfrescu-Pereira zamf@berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA Bjoern Hartmann bjoern@eecs.berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA ABSTRACT Pre-trained large language models (“LLMs”) like GPT-3 can engage in fuent, multi-turn instruction-taking out-of-the-box, making them attractive materials for designing natural language interactions. Using natural language to steer LLM outputs (“prompting”) has emerged as an important design technique potentially accessible to non-AI-experts. Crafting efective prompts can be challenging, however, and prompt-based interactions are brittle. Here, we explore whether non-AI-experts can successfully engage in “end-user prompt engineering” using a design probe—a prototype LLM-based chatbot design tool supporting development and systematic evaluation of prompting strategies. Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems.

3 METHOD: DESIGN PROBE In this work, we aim to understand how non-experts intuitively approach designing robust prompts, and whether and how they struggle in doing so. We want to dive deep into what those struggles reveal about people’s assumptions and understanding of promptbased systems in order to inform how end-user-facing prompt design tools might best support their users. We chose to investigate these questions in the context of designing instructional chatbots—chatbots that walk users through an activity (e.g., cooking a recipe, fxing a wif connection) while answering user questions and engaging in social conversation as needed. Chatbot tasks are sufciently open-ended that they open the door to a wide variety of types of problems and prompt-based solution approaches. Instructional chatbots represent a common chatbot use case (e.g., customer service bots), and their constituent tasks are some of the tasks that GPT-3 peforms more efectively out-of-the-box.

We chose to create a design probe because the robustness of prompt strategies is highly dependent on specifc conversational contexts, as is users’ ability to create prompts and debug. Enabling people to engage in designing LLM-and-prompt-based chatbots hands-on offers deeper insights than conducting interviews about hypothetical scenarios alone. We chose to purpose-build a prompt design tool because existing tools focus on enabling non-experts to experiment with various prompting strategies rather than crafting robust and generalizable prompts. 3.1 Designing a No-Code Prompt Design Tool as Probe Design Goals. We have two goals in designing BotDesigner: First, to enable end-users, without any prompt design experience or even programming or ML experience, to (i) create a chatbot using prompts, without code, and (ii) systematically evaluate their prompts. Second, to allow end-users to engage in this process in a fexible, open-ended way, allowing us to observe their intuitive behaviors and thought processes.

Examples of this advice include “try reframing that ‘do not’ statement into a positive statement, say what it is you want the bot to say, not what you don’t want it to say” or “have you considered copying some of the Carla-Lizzie transcript directly into the preamble?” We did not intentionally vary this advice across participants; however, due to the unpredictable nature of which errors participants chose to focus on, not all participants received the same advice or advice in the same order, a limitation of our approach. Analysis & Evaluation. We asked participants to think aloud, then engaged in exploratory data analysis, transcribing all videos and observing what prompt design approaches participants attempted, and noting when participants appeared to struggle and where interviewers intervened.

Systematic testing and robust prompt design—designing prompts that work across many users and many conversations—are by defnition impossible if the user only ever engages in a single conversation, even continuously updated. That said, for some contexts non-robust prompt design can be appropriate: chatbots intended for a single user who is also the designer do not necessarily need to be robust. A second major opportunity stems from the fact that most of the prompt design approaches participants tried before receiving any guidance (see §3.3 for details regarding this guidance) had some efect—enough for participants to feel that they could, in fact, afect chatbot output with prompt changes—but participants hit dead ends that incurred interviewer intervention more frequently than we expected. A searchable repository of examples, such as The DALL·E 2 Prompt Book [37], could help users overcome the “design”, “selection”, and “use” barriers that often led to the aforementioned dead ends.

Participants. All participants ( = 10) had little to no experience with prompt design; none had substantial prior experience 2Regression tests, in the context of software engineering and in the sense we intend here, are tests that verify that any new changes to a system do not reintroduce previously-resolved errors (called regressions). working with LLMs. We recruited participants with varying levels of programming and chatbot design experience. Recall that our focus here is understanding end-users in the domain of prompt design; experience in chatbot design was thus not considered grounds for exclusion. Our sample size was chosen in line with prior work around formative testing for usability [19, 43]: our goal is to explore the frst, “easy-to-fnd” problems users encounter when engaged in our task, and our experience with a pilot user suggested that problem discoverability was likely to be high. Our participant pool, skewed towards professionals and graduate students in STEM-related felds, is not representative of the population at large.

In this paper, we use chatbots as an example domain to explore the interactions between end user designers and prompt-based systems backed by LLMs (as BotDesigner is). A few additional limitations of our study bear exploration, and point to future studies. First, the reliance on a relatively small pool of likely “early adopters” drawn from academia may skew the observed phenomena towards a specifc set of analogies and preconceived notions around technology and its capabilities. We claim neither that our observations are universal of all end users, nor that they are a complete description of all common misconceptions or behaviors of end-users working with LLM-backed systems. Additionally, the time we gave participants to engage in prompt design was relatively limited, and it is likely that, given enough time and motivation, end users would advance quite quickly in developing better mental models and more efective strategies.
